# How to Use ChatGPT or Claude to Handle Government Paperwork

> **In short:** With free ChatGPT or Claude accounts, you can already decode dense government documents, draft official letters, and prepare for agency visits yourself. Cities around the world — including Polimill-backed municipalities in Japan — are testing similar tools, but you don't have to wait for yours to launch.

A government website sends you a 40-page PDF. The phone tree sends you to a different office. The form asks for information the instructions never explained. It's the kind of friction that wastes an afternoon — and it's exactly what a new generation of AI assistants is being built to fix. In Japan, the company Polimill is building AI tools for municipal governments; similar pilots are running in cities on several continents. Until those roll out to your town, though, you can do most of the work yourself today with tools you already have access to.

## What you'll need

- A **ChatGPT** (chatgpt.com) or **Claude** (claude.ai) account — free versions are fine for this.
- The confusing document itself, in text form. You can copy-paste from a PDF or webpage.
- About 10 minutes for your first attempt.

The steps below work the same way in either tool.

## Step 1 — Open a new chat and tell the AI what you're doing

Sign in to ChatGPT or Claude, then start a fresh conversation. A short opening line helps the AI give better answers, because it sets the context.

💬 Try this opener: *"I'm going to paste a government document. Help me understand what it actually requires me to do, in plain language."*

**You'll know it worked when** the AI responds by acknowledging the task and waiting for your paste.

## Step 2 — Paste the document and ask for a plain-language summary

Open the document (PDF, webpage, or letter), select the relevant text, and copy it. Then paste it directly into the chat and ask for a summary. The trick is asking for *plain language* — that's the part most people forget.

💬 Try this prompt: *"Explain this like I'm not a lawyer. In 3–4 sentences, what does this actually require me to do?"*

**You'll know it worked when** you get back a short, clear summary — usually two to five sentences — that you can read in one breath. If the answer is still long and full of jargon, push back: *"Shorter, please. Pretend I'm 12."*

## Step 3 — Ask one specific follow-up question at a time

Now read the summary and notice what's still unclear. Don't ask ten things at once — one focused question gets a much better answer.

💬 Try this prompt: *"What documents do I need to bring to apply for this?"* or *"What happens if I miss the deadline?"*

**You'll know it worked when** the AI returns a direct, single-paragraph answer. If it starts rambling or hedging, narrow the question further: *"Just the deadline — when is it?"*

## Step 4 — Draft a letter or email to the agency

When you need to write to an official, the AI can save you a lot of staring at a blank page. Tell it who you are, who you're writing to, and what you need — then let it draft.

💬 Try this prompt: *"Draft a polite email to my city's housing office asking about a delay in my application. My name is Jane, I applied on March 1, my case number is 12345. Keep it under 150 words."*

**You'll know it worked when** you have a draft that sounds like you after a small edit. Always read it out loud before sending — if a sentence doesn't sound like something you'd actually say, rewrite it in your own words.

## Step 5 — Decode jargon or translate a section you don't understand

Sometimes the problem isn't length — it's that one paragraph uses five-dollar words where a ten-cent word would do. The AI is great at this.

💬 Try this prompt: *"Rewrite this paragraph in plain English. Then list any words that sound legal or technical, and what they actually mean."*

**You'll know it worked when** you get a side-by-side: the plain version and a short glossary. That glossary is gold when you're reading the rest of the document on your own.

## Step 6 — Verify before you act

Here's the part most guides skip, and it's the most important. AI assistants sometimes **hallucinate** — they confidently make things up. They are very good at sounding right while being wrong. So before you submit a form, pay a fee, or change your behavior, double-check with the source.

💬 Try this prompt: *"Based on what we just discussed, list the 3 specific things I should confirm with the issuing agency before I act on this."*

**You'll know it worked when** the AI returns a short checklist. Call the office, check the official website, or visit in person — and only then take action.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Treating the AI's answer as the final word.** It's a starting point, not an authority. Always confirm deadlines, fees, and eligibility with the issuing agency.
- **Pasting personal information you don't need to share.** Strip out ID numbers, account numbers, and case-specific references before you paste. Use placeholders like "My case number is [X]" instead.
- **Asking vague questions.** "Explain this" is much weaker than "What does this regulation require me to do?" Specificity is everything.
- **Forgetting to read the AI's answer out loud.** If it doesn't sound like something a real person would say, the AI may be hallucinating — slow down and verify.

## What this means for you

- **If you deal with bureaucracy often:** This becomes your first stop before any phone call or office visit. You'll arrive prepared, with the right questions and the right documents.
- **If you're helping a parent or grandparent:** Sit with them, paste the confusing letter, and walk through the summary together. It's a small kindness that saves real frustration.
- **If you run a small business:** Permits, licensing, tax forms — all of it gets easier when you can decode the language before you commit to a course of action.

## Wrap-up

You don't need to wait for your city to launch an AI assistant. With a free ChatGPT or Claude account and the steps above, you can already cut through most of the friction — the long PDFs, the dense jargon, the blank-page letter. The trick is to use the AI as a translator and a drafter, never as the final authority. Open a chat, paste your document, and try Step 2 right now. The next time you're stuck on a form, you'll know exactly where to start.
